\chapter{Where French Changes Its Mind}
\label{ch:numbers-17-20}
\hlchaptermodality{15}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from seventeen to twenty in French, and name the two things that change at seventeen.}

At exactly seventeen, French stops inheriting numbers and starts building them — and swaps the order of the parts while doing it. seize is six-ten, fused; dix-sept is ten-seven, built out of two words you already own. Most language change is too slow to point at; this seam sits between two consecutive numbers and you can say both sides of it aloud. Then vingt arrives as a single inherited word again, and it is the number French will later count in: quatre-vingts, four twenties.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dix-sept]{dix-sept — seventeen}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-dix-sept}



\begin{quote}
Six words in a row arrived from Latin already welded. Here is the seventh, and you can read it at sight — which is exactly the surprise.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{dix-sept} = \emph{dees-SET}. The \textbf{x} of \emph{dix} becomes an \textbf{s} sound here, and the \textbf{p} of \emph{sept} is silent as always.
  \item \texttt{final-consonant} — the \textbf{t} of \emph{sept} \textbf{is} pronounced. That is unusual for a final consonant in French, and \emph{sept} keeps it in every position.
  \item Two words, one hyphen, one number.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
There is no Latin ancestor to trace here, and that is the point.

\textbf{dix-sept} is \textbf{dix} and \textbf{sept}, the two words you have had since the counting chapter, put side by side with a hyphen. Nothing has been worn down, nothing is hiding, nothing needs an etymology. It says \textbf{ten-seven} and it means seventeen.

Latin \emph{did} have a fused word for this — \emph{septendecim} — and French threw it away. After six inherited compounds the language simply stopped, and started building numbers out of parts the speaker already had.

You have just watched a language change its mind mid-count. The next lesson is about what exactly changed, because it is \textbf{two} things and not one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dix-sept\textquotedblright{} — \emph{dees-SET}, and the final \emph{t} is heard
  \item the seam — \textquotedblleft{}seize, dix-sept\textquotedblright{}; one is welded, one is built
  \item the parts — \textquotedblleft{}dix, sept, dix-sept\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say seventeen? (\textbf{dix-sept}, \emph{dees-SET}.) What two words is it made of? (\emph{\textbf{dix}} and \emph{\textbf{sept}}.) Did French inherit this one from Latin the way it inherited \emph{seize}? (\textbf{No} — Latin had \emph{septendecim} and French \textbf{abandoned} it, building the number out of parts instead.) Next: the two things that changed at this exact number.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[seize / dix-sept]{seize / dix-sept — the seam}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-seam}



\begin{quote}
Put the two words side by side — \textbf{seize}, then \textbf{dix-sept} — and something changed between them. Two things did, and most people only notice one.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: strategy and direction, both at once}]
The obvious change is \textbf{strategy}. Up to sixteen the numbers are \textbf{fused} — single words inherited whole and worn down. From seventeen they are \textbf{transparent} — built in the open out of words you already have.

The change nobody notices is \textbf{direction}, and it is a question of which half comes first:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{shape} & \textbf{what comes first} \\
\midrule
seize & \emph{sē-decim}, fused & the \textbf{digit}: six-ten \\
dix-sept & \emph{dix} + \emph{sept}, built & the \textbf{ten}: ten-seven \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Seize} is \textbf{six-ten}. \emph{Dix-sept} is \textbf{ten-seven}. The two halves have swapped places. So at exactly one number, French changed \textbf{how} it makes the word and \textbf{which way round} the parts go — and it never went back.

That is worth seeing because it is a rare thing to catch. Languages usually change too slowly to point at. Here the join is visible between two consecutive numbers, and you can say both sides of it out loud.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item across the seam — \textquotedblleft{}seize, dix-sept\textquotedblright{}
  \item the first change — \textquotedblleft{}fused, then built\textquotedblright{}
  \item the second change — \textquotedblleft{}six-ten, then ten-seven\textquotedblright{}
  \item the summary — \textquotedblleft{}at seventeen, both the method and the order flipped\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the \textbf{two} things that change between \emph{seize} and \emph{dix-sept}. (The \textbf{strategy} — fused becomes built; and the \textbf{direction} — digit-first becomes ten-first.) Which half comes first in \emph{seize}? (The \textbf{digit}: six-ten.) And in \emph{dix-sept}? (The \textbf{ten}: ten-seven.) Next: eighteen, which now costs you nothing.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dix-huit]{dix-huit — eighteen}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-dix-huit}



\begin{quote}
This is the first number in the book that costs you nothing. You already know the rule; this is just applying it.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{dix-huit} = \emph{dee-ZWEET}. The \textbf{x} of \emph{dix} buzzes into a \textbf{z} here, because \emph{huit} begins with a vowel sound.
  \item \texttt{silent-h} — the \textbf{h} of \emph{huit} is not said, which is why the \emph{z} can carry straight across into it.
  \item The final \textbf{t} of \emph{huit} \textbf{is} pronounced.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dix + huit}, ten and eight. Nothing more.

What is worth a moment is what Latin did here instead, because it is stranger than anything French does. For 18 and 19 Latin did not add — it \textbf{subtracted}. Eighteen was \textbf{duodēvīgintī}: \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{two from twenty}.\textquotedblright{} Nineteen was \emph{ūndēvīgintī}, \textquotedblleft{}one from twenty.\textquotedblright{}

Every language descended from Latin dropped that. French, Spanish and Italian all count \textbf{up} to twenty rather than down from it. So the plain \emph{ten-eight} in front of you is not a lazy simplification — it is the survivor of a competition, and the elegant subtraction trick is the thing that lost.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dix-huit\textquotedblright{} — \emph{dee-ZWEET}, the \emph{x} buzzing into the vowel
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}dix-sept, dix-huit\textquotedblright{}; hear \emph{dees-} then \emph{dee-z-}
  \item what Latin said — \textquotedblleft{}two from twenty\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say eighteen? (\textbf{dix-huit}, \emph{dee-ZWEET}.) Why does the \emph{x} buzz here but hiss in \emph{dix-sept}? (\emph{\textbf{huit}} begins with a \textbf{vowel sound}; \emph{sept} does not.) How did Latin build eighteen? (By \textbf{subtracting} — \emph{duodē- vīgintī}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{two from twenty}\textquotedblright{}.) Did French keep that? (\textbf{No.}) Next: nineteen.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dix-neuf]{dix-neuf — nineteen}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-dix-neuf}



\begin{quote}
The last of the built teens — and a word that quietly means two different things.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{dix-neuf} = \emph{dees-NUF}. The \textbf{x} hisses as an \textbf{s} here, the way it does in \emph{dix-sept}, because \emph{neuf} begins with a consonant.
  \item The \textbf{eu} is the rounded vowel you made in \textbf{sœur}: lips rounded, tongue forward.
  \item The final \textbf{f} is pronounced.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dix + neuf}, ten and nine.

The interesting part is \textbf{neuf} itself, which is two words wearing one coat:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{neuf} = \textbf{nine}, from Latin \emph{novem}
  \item \textbf{neuf} = \textbf{new}, from Latin \emph{novus}
\end{itemize}

Those were distinct in Latin and French wore them into the same four letters. So \emph{un livre neuf} is \textquotedblleft{}a new book,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{neuf livres} is \textquotedblleft{}nine books,\textquotedblright{} and only the position tells you which.

They are not unrelated, either. The same \emph{nov-} is behind English \textbf{novel}, \textbf{novice}, \textbf{innovate} and \textbf{November} — the old \textbf{ninth} month, which is the counting month you already met. \emph{Novem} and \emph{novus} are cousins from far enough back that nobody is quite sure which sense came first.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dix-neuf\textquotedblright{} — \emph{dees-NUF}, the \emph{f} heard
  \item all three built teens — \textquotedblleft{}dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf\textquotedblright{}
  \item the double word — \textquotedblleft{}neuf is nine, and neuf is new\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say nineteen? (\textbf{dix-neuf}, \emph{dees-NUF}.) What are its two parts? (\emph{\textbf{dix}} and \emph{\textbf{neuf}}.) What else does \textbf{neuf} mean besides nine? (\textbf{New} — from \emph{novus}, where the number is from \emph{novem}.) Which month carries the same \emph{nov-}? (\textbf{novembre}.) Next: twenty, and a different system again.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vingt]{vingt — twenty}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-vingt}



\begin{quote}
Three built numbers in a row, and then this — which is not built out of anything at all.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{vingt} = \emph{VA(N)}. The \textbf{in} is the nasal vowel you have in \textbf{vin} and \textbf{pain}.
  \item \texttt{silent-final} — the \textbf{g} and the \textbf{t} are both silent. Four written letters after the vowel, none of them heard.
  \item Say \textbf{vin} and \textbf{vingt} aloud: standing alone they are \textbf{identical}. Only the spelling and the sentence tell them apart.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{vingt} is Latin \textbf{vīgintī}, and that is the whole story: an old, single, inherited word, like \emph{dix} and unlike \emph{dix-sept}.

So the count you have just walked through has \textbf{three} systems in it, not two:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item 11–16 — inherited, \textbf{fused}, digit first
  \item 17–19 — \textbf{built}, transparent, ten first
  \item 20 — inherited again, a \textbf{single word} built from nothing
\end{itemize}

Twenty is not the end of a pattern. It is the start of a different one, because \emph{vingt} is the number French will later count \textbf{in}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vingt\textquotedblright{} — \emph{VA(N)}, everything after the vowel silent
  \item the homophones — \textquotedblleft{}vin, vingt\textquotedblright{}; identical on their own
  \item the last four — \textquotedblleft{}dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf, vingt\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say twenty? (\textbf{vingt}, \emph{VA(N)}.) How many of its letters after the vowel are pronounced? (\textbf{None.}) Which word from the table chapter sounds exactly the same? (\emph{\textbf{vin}}, wine.) Is \emph{vingt} built out of smaller numbers? (\textbf{No} — it is a single inherited word, from \emph{vīgintī}.) Next: what that \emph{vīgintī} went on to do.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vīgintī]{vīgintī — the number French counts in}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-vigesimal}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Vingt} looks like an ending. It is a beginning, and this lesson is here so that a famous French oddity is already explained before you meet it.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{vīgintī} did not only give French \emph{vingt}. It gave English a word for an idea:

\textbf{vigesimal} — counting in \textbf{twenties}, the way \emph{decimal} is counting in tens.

Most of Europe counts in tens. But a way of counting in \textbf{twenties} survived underneath French, and it surfaces in the higher numbers. Eighty in French is not \textquotedblleft{}eight-ten.\textquotedblright{} It is:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{quatre-vingts} — literally \textbf{four twenties}
\end{quote}

Four twenties is eighty. And ninety-nine, famously, is \emph{quatre-vingt-dix-neuf} — \textquotedblleft{}four twenties, ten, nine.\textquotedblright{}

You are not learning those numbers here. You are learning \textbf{why} they will look the way they do, so that when they arrive they are a consequence rather than a shock. English keeps one fossil of the same habit: a \textbf{score} is twenty, and \textquotedblleft{}four score and seven years ago\textquotedblright{} is \emph{quatre-vingt-sept} in a different language.

So \emph{vingt} is the base of a second counting system hiding inside a decimal one — which is a much better thing to know at twenty than at eighty.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the English word — \textquotedblleft{}vigesimal: counting by twenties\textquotedblright{}
  \item the preview — \textquotedblleft{}quatre-vingts, four twenties, eighty\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English fossil — \textquotedblleft{}four score and seven\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{vigesimal} mean? (\textbf{Counting by twenties.}) What does \emph{quatre-vingts} literally say, and what number is it? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Four twenties}\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{eighty}.) Which English word for twenty preserves the same habit? (A \textbf{score}.) Next: all ten numbers together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — across the seam, and up to twenty}

\label{lesson:FR-C12-practice-seam}



\begin{quote}
You can now count to twenty. Run the whole thing, and listen for the place where the machine changes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: the full count}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item eleven to twenty — \textquotedblleft{}onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize, dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf, vingt\textquotedblright{}
  \item from one, the whole way
  \item the four new ones alone — \textquotedblleft{}dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf, vingt\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf, vingt\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn: hear the seam}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two words either side — \textquotedblleft{}seize, dix-sept\textquotedblright{}
  \item what changed first — \textquotedblleft{}fused, then built\textquotedblright{}
  \item what changed second — \textquotedblleft{}six-ten, then ten-seven\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the x that cannot decide}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hissing — \textquotedblleft{}dix-sept, dix-neuf\textquotedblright{}; both follow a consonant
  \item buzzing — \textquotedblleft{}dix-huit\textquotedblright{}; it follows a vowel sound
  \item the reason aloud — \textquotedblleft{}the x buzzes into a vowel and hisses before a consonant\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{four numbers}, seventeen to twenty, and with them the whole count to 20.
  \item \textbf{a seam you can point at} — at seventeen French changed both its \textbf{strategy} and its \textbf{direction}, and never went back. Most language change is too slow to witness; this one sits between two consecutive numbers.
  \item \textbf{three systems in ten numbers} — inherited and fused, built and transparent, then a single inherited word again at \emph{vingt}.
  \item \textbf{an oddity explained before you meet it} — \emph{vīgintī} is why eighty will be \textbf{quatre-vingts}, four twenties.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count from eleven to twenty without stopping. Which number is the seam, and what two things change there? (\textbf{Seventeen} — \textbf{fused becomes built}, and \textbf{digit-first becomes ten-first}.) Why does the \emph{x} of \emph{dix} buzz in \emph{dix-huit} but hiss in \emph{dix-neuf}? (\emph{\textbf{huit}} begins with a \textbf{vowel sound}.) What will \emph{quatre-vingts} mean, and why? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Four twenties}\textquotedblright{} — eighty; from \emph{vīgintī}, the \textbf{vigesimal} habit.)
\end{tcolorbox}
